analysis.one_liner: Forces Medicare drug plans to open pharmacy networks and strips drug middlemen of hidden price-based fees.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan PBM overhaul with 70 cosponsors has sat in three House committees without a hearing or vote since July 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and build pharmacy networks for insurers. It would require Medicare drug plans to let any pharmacy that meets standard terms join their networks, set federal standards for fair pharmacy contracts, and ban PBMs from keeping any income beyond flat, disclosed service fees — including the practice of pocketing part of rebates or the gap between what a plan pays and what a pharmacy receives. It also forces detailed annual reporting on drug prices, rebates, and affiliate pharmacies in both Medicare and employer health plans, with civil fines for violations. The bill was referred to three House committees and has not received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and people in employer health plans, who would get clearer information about what their drugs really cost and what middlemen keep. Independent and community pharmacies — including rural pharmacies that are often the only one for miles — would gain the right to join insurance networks and protection from retaliation when they report unfair contract terms. Employers and Medicare plans would gain the power to audit their PBMs and claw back money the PBM kept improperly.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare drug plans to let any willing pharmacy that meets standard contract terms join the network, and directs the Health Secretary to set standards for 'reasonable and relevant' contract terms with an enforcement process pharmacies can use to file complaints.

Bars pharmacy benefit managers from earning any income other than bona fide, flat-dollar service fees, and requires rebates and discounts from drugmakers to be fully passed through to the plan; PBMs must disgorge anything improperly kept.

Requires detailed annual reports from PBMs to plans and the government on drug prices, rebates, what pharmacies are paid, the share of prescriptions steered to PBM-owned pharmacies, and total revenue the PBM and its affiliates retained.

Extends similar transparency rules to pharmacy benefit managers serving employer group health plans, with a plain-language summary beneficiaries can request and civil penalties of $10,000 per day for failing to report.

Requires reports on 'essential retail pharmacies' — including rural and underserved-area pharmacies — tracking their reimbursement, network participation, and closure trends, and funds enforcement at CMS, the Inspector General, and MedPAC.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them bear the direct cost: they lose fee structures tied to drug prices, must pass through rebates, pay for annual reporting, reimburse sponsors for penalties, and face disgorgement and fines. Taxpayers fund roughly $322 million in new appropriations for oversight. Drug plans and PBMs also face new compliance and audit burdens that could add administrative costs to premiums.

drawbacks.text: The 'any willing pharmacy' mandate and contract standards limit plans' ability to run smaller, discounted preferred networks, which is one tool plans use to hold premiums down — some of the compliance and reimbursement costs could flow back to beneficiaries through higher premiums.

The bill does not ban the rebate system itself: a PBM may still receive rebates calculated as a percentage of a drug's price so long as they are fully passed through, leaving the manufacturer-rebate model that pushes list prices up largely intact.
It appropriates about $322 million in new federal spending for CMS, the HHS Inspector General, and MedPAC to carry out the oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For anyone who fills prescriptions, the transparency and pass-through provisions attack a documented problem: middlemen whose pay grows when drug prices grow, and independent pharmacies closing partly because reimbursement falls short of their costs. The main honest objections are that network-opening rules can raise premiums by limiting plans' negotiating leverage, and that leaving percentage-based rebates in place (only requiring pass-through) preserves the upstream pricing game. Those are real but secondary to the core shift of forcing middlemen's economics into the open.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025 and referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means — and none has scheduled a hearing or vote, so it is sitting with no path to the floor yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA), a pharmacist, introduced the bill on July 10, 2025 with original cosponsors from both parties, including Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-MI).
The bill was referred simultaneously to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees, which requires all three to act on their portions before the bill can advance.
It collected 70 cosponsors — 39 of 223 House Republicans and 31 of 217 House Democrats — but the action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action beyond the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them are better off so far: the status quo of opaque fees and closed pharmacy networks stays in place while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBM middlemen and their insurer owners

for.name: Rep. Buddy Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original Democratic cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and have scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote in the months since.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent insurers
against.role: Largest PBMs (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts/Cigna, Optum Rx/UnitedHealth)
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed and lobbied against standalone PBM reform measures that would bar price-based fees and force rebate pass-through.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship splits almost evenly — 39 Republicans and 31 Democrats — and no floor or committee vote has occurred, so no party-line pattern has formed yet.

industries.note: The bill bans PBMs from keeping anything but flat, disclosed service fees, requires full pass-through of manufacturer rebates, allows plan audits, and forces them to disgorge improperly kept money and reimburse sponsors for penalties. Their revenue has historically grown with drug prices and opaque fee structures, which is exactly what the bill targets.

PBMs and their affiliates must disclose what share of prescriptions they steer to their own pharmacies and the price gap versus independent pharmacies in the same network. Plans and beneficiaries would see the steering and spread for the first time.

Any willing pharmacy can join Medicare drug networks, contract terms must meet federal standards, reimbursement adequacy gets tracked for rural and underserved-area pharmacies, and an anti-retaliation process protects pharmacies that report violations. These are typically small businesses, not a concentrated interest.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: Plans gain the right to audit their PBMs, receive disgorged money, and see true net drug costs, but they take on compliance obligations and could face higher pharmacy reimbursement under the contract standards. Insurers that own PBMs sit on the losing side of the same provision.

Rebates must be fully passed through to plans rather than intermediated by PBMs, but manufacturers' rebate contracts with PBMs must be explained in writing to plan sponsors, which could pressure formulary-placement deals that favor higher-priced brand drugs.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to three committees with no scheduled hearing rarely move on their own; the realistic path for this one is having its provisions folded into a larger health or Medicare package where PBM reforms have advanced before, rather than getting a standalone floor vote.
